Chapter 7: Navigating Conflict with Personality Awareness
Let’s face it—conflict is something we all run into. But what if I told you that understanding personality can actually change the way we experience and resolve disagreements? Instead of seeing conflict as a threat, we can start to see it as a chance to get to know what really matters to each of us.
Here’s the first thing to keep in mind: our style of dealing with conflict usually comes from our personality. Maybe you’re someone who likes to tackle issues head-on, hoping to fix things right away. Or maybe you prefer to step back and sort through your feelings before talking things out. Neither way is better or worse—they’re just different ways of coping.
Imagine conflict as a dance. Each of us moves to our own rhythm. Sometimes, those rhythms don’t match up, and that’s when frustration can sneak in. But if you’re willing to listen for the other person’s tempo, you might discover a new way to move together and find some common ground.
So, what can you actually do when conflict pops up? Let’s break it down into a few practical steps:
Pause and Reflect. Before you react, take a second to check in with yourself. Are you the type to avoid confrontation, jump right in, or maybe try to smooth things over? And what about the other person—can you guess their style?
Name the Pattern. It can help to gently point out what’s happening. You might say, “I notice I tend to withdraw when things get tense, and I wonder if that makes it harder for us to resolve things.” This simple step can shift the whole conversation.
Seek Understanding. Try asking open questions, like, “Can you help me understand what feels most important to you right now?” It’s amazing how much clarity you can gain just by listening.
Agree on Process. Decide together how you want to approach the issue. Maybe you need a break, maybe you want to set a specific time to talk, or maybe writing things down first helps.
Now, let’s talk about how this works in real life—like at work. Maybe there’s someone on your team who values harmony so much, they keep quiet even when there’s a problem. Over time, that can turn into resentment. But if everyone recognizes and respects each other’s conflict styles, it creates space for every voice, and small issues don’t have a chance to grow into big problems.
In close relationships, understanding these patterns can make it much easier to forgive and grow together. When both people realize that a lot of their reactions are just part of their personality—not a matter of willpower or intent—it’s a lot easier to move past blame and start working toward real resolution.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the goal isn’t to get rid of conflict altogether. It’s about moving through it with more awareness and compassion. When we do that, our relationships get stronger, and they feel a whole lot more genuine.
